Chapter 4: Cross Sections

4 Cross Sections

  • Cross sections are how physicists analyze collider data (such as the exabytes of LHC data that is collected every year)
(d𝜎dΩ)CM=164𝜋2𝐸CM2|ℳ︀|2

and the Born approximation

(d𝜎dΩ)Born=𝑚𝑒24𝜋2[𝑉̃(𝑘⃗)]2
  • Cross sections used to make sense of particle accelerator data

  • Cross sectional area:

    𝜎=#︎particlestime×number density×velocity of beam=1𝑇1Φ𝑁,Φ=#︎density×beam vel.=1𝑉×|𝑣⃗|

    • More useful/natural is differential cross section

      d𝜎dΩ
      for some angle/change in angle Ω.
    • Info about shape of object with this
4.0.0.1 QM
  • Generalize to Differential Cross Sections due to their changing based on angle in colliders

  • In QM, there is a probability of scattering

    𝑃=𝑁𝑁inc
    with 𝑁inc number of incident particles

  • Cross section

    𝑑𝜎=1𝑇1Φ𝑑𝑃
    (normalize flux)

  • Differential scattering number

    d𝑁=𝐿×d𝜎
    • 𝐿 is defined as the Luminosity through this equation

4.0.1 Cross Section to Matrix Element

  • 2→𝑁 Particle Interaction:

    𝑝1+𝑝2→{𝑝𝑗}
  • Φ=|𝑣⃗1−𝑣⃗2|𝑉⟹d𝜎=𝑉𝑇1|𝑣⃗1−𝑣⃗2|d𝑃

  • Have that

    d𝑃=|⟨𝑓|𝑆|𝑖⟩|2⟨𝑓|𝑓⟩⟨𝑖|𝑖⟩dΠ

    • with

      dΠ=∏𝑗𝑁(2𝜋)3d3𝑝𝑗
    • ∫dΠ=1

      since

      ∫d𝑃(2𝜋)=1𝑉
  • [𝑎𝑝,𝑎𝑞†]=(2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝−𝑞)
    • Implies that ⟨𝑝|𝑝⟩=(2𝜋)3𝛿3(0)

    • Normally 𝛿3(0) is infinite but

      (2𝜋)3𝛿3(𝑝)=∫𝑉d3𝑥𝑒𝑖𝑝⃗⋅𝑥⃗⟹𝛿3(0)=𝑉(2𝜋)3and𝛿4(0)=𝑇𝑉(2𝜋)4
  • ⟨𝑝|𝑝⟩=2𝜔𝑝𝑉=2𝐸𝑝𝑉

    • It is also implied that

      ⟨𝑓|𝑓⟩=∏𝑗2𝐸𝑗𝑉

4.0.2 Actually Calculating the S-matrix (perturbatively)

  • Notice that the first order of a S-matrix is just 𝟙 since that is the case in which nothing happens

  • Write 𝑆=𝟙+𝑖𝒯︀

    • 𝒯︀≡ transfer matrix
    • 𝒯︀ implies momentum conservation since it vanishes unless |𝑖⟩ and |𝑓⟩ have the same 4-momentum
  • 𝒯︀=(2𝜋)4𝛿4(Σ𝑝)ℳ︀
4.0.2.1 Matrix Elements

  • ⟨𝑓|𝑆−𝟙|𝑖⟩=𝑖(2𝜋)4𝛿4(Σ𝑃)⟨𝑓|ℳ︀|𝑖⟩

    • |⟨𝑓|𝑆|𝑖⟩|2=𝛿4(0)𝛿4(Σ𝑝)(2𝜋)8|⟨𝑓|𝑀|𝑖⟩|2=𝛿4(Σ𝑝)𝑇𝑉(2𝜋)4|ℳ︀|2

4.0.3 Lorentz Invariant Phase Space

  • We denote the differential dΠLIPS as being defined as the product over final momenta differentials times delta function factors, that is

    𝑑ΠLIPS≡∏final 𝑗d3𝑝𝑗(2𝜋)312𝐸𝑝𝑗(2𝜋)4𝛿4(Σ𝑝)

  • Utilizing this, (as well as the derived S-matrix elements from earlier) we can write the differential probability d𝑝 via

    d𝑃=|⟨𝑓|𝑆|𝑖⟩|2⟨𝑓|𝑓⟩⟨𝑖|𝑖⟩dΠ=(2𝜋)4𝛿4(Σ𝑝)×𝑇𝑉2𝐸1𝑉×2𝐸2𝑉×1Π𝑗(2𝐸𝑗𝑉)|ℳ︁|2∏𝑗d3𝑝𝑗(2𝜋)3𝑉=𝑇12𝐸1×2𝐸2|ℳ︁|2dΠLIPS

  • This easily gives us the cross section for 2→𝑗 decay:

    d𝜎=1(2𝐸1)(2𝐸2)|𝑣⃗1−𝑣⃗2||ℳ︁|2dΠLIPS

4.0.4 Particle Decay Rate

  • This is another useful quantity in analyzing accelerator data denoted by dΓ

  • The definition for this decay rate is dΓ≡1𝑇d𝑃 (probability of decay in certain amount of time)

    • Specifically it is the probability that a particle of momentum 𝑝1 decays into particles of momenta 𝑝𝑗 in a time 𝑇
    • S-matrix theory cannot be used to describe these decays (?)
  • dΓ=12𝐸1|ℳ︁|2dΠLIPS

4.0.5 Cross Section formula

  • Consider 2→2 Scattering

    • This means that the momenta are 𝑝1+𝑝2→𝑝3+𝑝4

  • In the center of mass frame, the net momentum for each is zero. Therefore 𝒑1=−𝒑2, 𝒑3=−𝒑4 which implies that 𝐸1+𝐸2=𝐸3+𝐸4≡𝐸CM

  • Then, for the LIPS differential, we get that

    dΠLIPS=(2𝜋)4𝛿4(Σ𝑝)d3𝑝3(2𝜋)312𝐸3d3𝑝4(2𝜋)312𝐸4

  • This is equivalent to the integral

    dΠLIPS=116𝜋2dΩ∫d𝑝𝑓𝑝𝑓2𝐸31𝐸4𝛿(𝐸3+𝐸4−𝐸CM)

    (I don’t understand how this is true)

    • Where 𝑝𝑓=|𝒑𝟑|=|𝒑𝟒| and 𝐸3=𝑚32+𝑝𝑓2, 𝐸4=𝑚42+𝑝𝑓2
    • Notice that the energies are dependent on the final momentum 𝑝𝑓, and so this integral is in fact, not trivial.

  • Now we conduct a change of variables from 𝑝𝑓 to 𝑥(𝑝𝑓)≡𝐸3(𝑝𝑓)+𝐸4(𝑝𝑓)−𝐸CM

    • Calculating the change of variables, we get

      d𝑥d𝑝𝑓=dd𝑝𝑓(𝐸3+𝐸4−𝐸CM)=𝑝𝑓𝐸3+𝑝𝑓𝐸4=𝐸3+𝐸4𝐸3𝐸4𝑝𝑓

  • We also have that

    𝐸3+𝐸4=𝐸CM

  • Then,

    dΠLIPS=116𝜋2dΩ∫𝑚3+𝑚4−𝐸CM∞d𝑥𝑝𝑓𝐸CM𝛿(𝑥)=116𝜋2dΩ𝑝𝑓𝐸CM𝜃(𝐸CM−𝑚3−𝑚4)

    where 𝜃(𝑥) is the Heaviside step function due to the integral of the delta function.

  • Putting this all together, we obtain that

    d𝜎=1(2𝐸1)(2𝐸2)|𝒗1−𝒗2|116𝜋2dΩ𝑝𝑓𝐸CM|ℳ︁|2𝜃(𝐸CM−𝑚3−𝑚4)

    • Using

      |𝒗1−𝒗2|=||𝒑1|𝐸1+|𝒑2|𝐸2|=|𝒑𝑖|𝐸CM𝐸1𝐸2

      , we obtain that, under the condition that the masses are equivalent,

      (d𝜎dΩ)CM=164𝜋2𝐸CM2|ℳ︁|2
      as desired, allowing for computation of cross sections for simple scattering based off of quantum field theory predictions for |ℳ︁|2

4.0.6 Born Approximation

  • The Born approximation is a special case where a scalar electron 𝜙𝑒 with mass 𝑚𝑒 scatters off of a scalar proton 𝜙𝑝 with mass 𝑚𝑝

    • It is considered the nonrelativistic limit

  • I will not derive the born approximation, however, it is given by the formula

    (d𝜎dΩ)Born≡𝑚𝑒24𝜋2[𝑉̃(𝑘⃗)]2

    where 𝑉̃ is the fourier transformed potential/the potential in fourier space.

    • 𝑉̃(𝐾⃗)=∫d3𝑥𝑒−𝑖𝑘⃗⋅𝑥⃗𝑉(𝑥⃗)
